rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain weakly retained compounds while promoting elution of all 10 compounds. The retention and resolution patterns will guide subsequent changes to gradient range, duration, and temperature.
Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing the available resolution margin. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.
Raise temperature to test whether selectivity changes can separate the crowded middle peaks while preserving the short elution time. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect.

Test a smaller temperature increase to improve the remaining critical pair while monitoring the narrowing gap between earlier middle peaks. The unchanged gradient should keep the time penalty at zero.

Slightly lengthen the gradient to improve the newly limiting middle-peak separation while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region. This will also test whether the other close pair retains sufficient resolution.

Test a slightly shallower gradient by lowering the final organic fraction, seeking another maximum-score method with improved separation of the earlier critical pair. Monitor the later critical pair and last-peak time, since both are close to their score thresholds.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction for an alternative maximum-score method. This probes whether elution can be accelerated while preserving resolution of both critical pairs.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover the resolution lost with the higher starting organic fraction. This may provide another maximum-score method with a better-balanced margin between the two critical pairs and no time penalty.

Lower the endpoint one more grid step to bring the limiting resolution above 1.5 while retaining adequate separation of the other critical pair. The projected last-peak time is near 8 minutes, so this tests another potential maximum-score method.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so explore a substantially cooler temperature for an alternative selectivity regime. This tests whether temperature-driven elution-order changes can resolve the middle cluster with the shorter gradient.

With the maximum score already secured, test a faster, hotter alternative that may move the middle peaks beyond their selectivity crossover. This probes whether full resolution can be recovered at substantially shorter retention times.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a moderately longer gradient to adjust selectivity and spread the crowded middle peaks at 60 C. This explores a faster alternative to the established maximum-score method.

Increase the starting organic fraction to test whether the remaining critical pair separates further on the high-temperature side of its elution-order crossover. Monitor early-peak compression while retaining the short gradient.

Return to the successful 55 C selectivity regime, using a longer gradient to improve middle-peak resolution and a higher starting organic fraction to offset retention time. This tests another potential maximum-score method while avoiding the early-peak compression seen at phi0 0.20.

Preserve injection 5’s successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute while ending the gradient earlier. Because all peaks previously eluted before this new gradient endpoint reaches the outlet, the separation should remain unchanged and retain the maximum CRF.

Keep the proven gradient slope and temperature while shortening the programmed gradient to 8 minutes. All peaks should still elute before the endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, preserving the maximum-score separation.

Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to target resolution above 1.5 for both critical pairs while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes. This may provide a maximum-score alternative with more balanced resolution and time margins.

Maintain the proven gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the final compound can still elute within the zero-time-penalty window while preserving the critical separations.

Injection 18 shows that the zero-time-penalty region extends beyond 8 minutes. Slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 9 to improve the earlier critical pair while testing whether the later pair remains above 1.5 and the time penalty stays zero.

Lengthen injection 14’s gradient to improve its limiting middle-pair resolution while retaining the stronger separation of the later critical pair. The projected last-peak time is about 8.6 minutes, testing another potential maximum-score method.

Slightly flatten injection 20’s gradient to raise its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The estimated last-peak time is near 9 minutes, so this also tests the boundary of the zero-time-penalty region.

Match injection 9’s successful gradient slope with a shorter programmed gradient and lower endpoint. The last peak should elute before the endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, preserving its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of 1.58.

Slightly flatten injection 19’s gradient to test the neighboring maximum-score region. The earlier critical pair should gain resolution, while the later pair and last-peak time will determine whether the CRF remains 1.000.

Test a shorter gradient followed by a hold to determine whether the endpoint can improve the final-peak time without sacrificing the middle-pair separations. This is an exploratory alternative; the maximum CRF is already secured by several methods.

Use a gradient slope between the maximum-score methods from injections 19 and 23, targeting both critical resolutions above 1.5 and a last-peak time near 8.3 minutes. This final alternative is expected to retain CRF 1.000, the maximum already achieved.
